messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo Energy Harvester (PEH) interface.
    *   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ (from `out` to `0`) with $V_{out}$ between 1.8V and 3.6V.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8$ V (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6$ V (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05$ V (Ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4$ s (Startup)
        *   $dv \le 0.02$ V (Settled)
    *   Piezo Model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30 nF) and $R_{leak}$ (20 MOhm).
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx 3.2$ V.

    *   S1 (Nominal): $I_p = 50\mu\text{A}, f = 100\text{Hz}, R_L = 330\text{k}\Omega$.
    *   S2 (Heavy Load): $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$. (FBR failed $V_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$)
    *   S3 (Strong Excitation, Light Load): $I_p = 100\mu\text{A}, R_L = 2.2\text{M}\Omega$. (FBR failed $V_{max}$, ripple, and settled)
    *   S4 (Weak Excitation): $I_p = 30\mu\text{A}, R_L = 1\text{M}\Omega$. (FBR failed $V_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$)
    *   S5 (Low Frequency): $f = 80\text{Hz}, R_L = 470\text{k}\Omega$. (FBR failed settled)
    *   S6 (Hot): $C_p = 30\text{nF}, R_L = 330\text{k}\Omega$. (FBR OK)

    *   The FBR is a passive rectifier.
    *   S2 failure ($V_{avg} < 1.8$V): The rectifier drop and the heavy load reduce the average voltage.
    *   S3 failure ($V_{max} > 3.6$V): No voltage regulation. High $I_p$ and light load drive $V_{out}$ too high.
    *   S4 failure ($V_{avg} < 1.8$V): Insufficient energy to overcome diode drops and power the load.

    *   *Option A: SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor)*. This is the gold standard for piezo energy harvesting. It flips the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks to maximize energy extraction.
        *   Structure: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ Buffer. Or an inverter before the rectifier.
        *   Standard SSHI: Piezo $C_p$ is flipped using an inductor $L$ and a switch.
    *   *Option B: Active Rectification (Synchronous)*. Replacing diodes with switches. But we have limited switches (4) and SYNC controllers (2).
    *   *Option C: Zener Clamp*. To fix the $V_{max}$ issue in S3, a Zener diode (DZ33) on the output is essential.
    *   *Option D: Buck/Boost Converter*. Probably too complex for the component count and the specific SYNC constraints.

    *   The piezo is basically a capacitor $C_p$ being charged/discharged by $I_p$.
    *   We want to extract the energy. A simple bridge rectifier (FBR) does this, but the "voltage" on $C_p$ oscillates around $V_{out}$.
    *   SSHI (specifically SECE - Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) or simple inductive flipping helps.
    *   Let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" or "Series-SSHI" inspired topology.
    *   Wait, looking at the SYNC controller: it closes switches for `ton` at extrema. This is perfect for an inductor-based flip.
    *   Topology proposal 1: SSHI-like inverter before a bridge.
        *   Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ connected in parallel to the piezo to flip the charge.
        *   Then a diode bridge to charge $C_{out}$.
        *   Wait, the "standard" SSHI flips the piezo voltage *before* the rectification or as part of it.
        *   Simple Inductive Flip: $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo. When $S$ closes, $C_p$ and $L$ resonate, flipping the voltage. This increases the voltage swing across the diodes.
    *   Actually, a simpler approach to fix FBR is to add a Zener clamp (for S3) and maybe use an inductive boost or a better rectifier.

    *   **Design 1: FBR + Zener + Buffer Cap**. (Baseline fix)
        *   FBR (4x DSCH)
        *   $C_{out}$ (large)
        *   Zener (DZ33) to ground.
        *   *Critique*: This won't fix S2/S4 (insufficient voltage) since the diode drops are still there.

    *   **Design 2: SSHI (Parallel)**.
        *   Piezo $\rightarrow$ Bridge $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
        *   Add $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   When the piezo reaches its peak, the switch $S$ closes, flipping the charge.
        *   This increases the voltage available to the rectifier.
        *   Components: 4x D (Bridge), 1x L, 1x S, 1x SYNC, 1x C (output), 1x DZ33 (Zener).
        *   Wait, if $L$ and $S$ are in parallel with the piezo, does it flip? Yes, $C_p$ resonates with $L$.
        *   Let's refine:
            *   Piezo terminals: pzp, pzn.
            *   S1: [pzp, n1], L1: [n1, pzn], Ctrl: G1. (Wait, that's a series combo).
            *   Better: $S$ and $L$ in series, then that combo in parallel with the piezo.
            *   S1: [pzp, n1], L1: [n1, pzn], Ctrl: G1. This is a loop. When S1 closes, pzp-L1-S1-pzn is a loop.
            *   Then the bridge: D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn]. (Standard FBR).

    *   **Design 3: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction)**.
        *   Piezo $C_p$ charges an intermediate capacitor $C_{ext}$ via a switch.
        *   $C_{ext}$ then dumps into the output via a diode.
        *   This is often more efficient than FBR.
        *   Components: S1 (pzp, n1), C1 (n1, 0), D1 (n1, out), etc.
        *   Since we have 2 SYNCs and 4 switches, we can do this.

    *   FBR failed S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation). This means we need more "voltage boost" or better efficiency.
    *   SSHI flipping increases the average voltage delivered to the output.
    *   S3 failed $V_{max}$. A Zener (DZ33) is mandatory.

    *   S1: [pzp, n1], L1: [n1, pzn], G1: SYNC (edges="both", ton=pi*sqrt(L*Cp)).
    *   Bridge:
        *   D1: [pzp, out] (DSCH)
        *   D2: [pzn, out] (DSCH)
        *   D3: [0, pzp] (DSCH)
        *   D4: [0, pzn] (DSCH)
    *   Storage:
        *   Cout: [out, 0]
    *   Clamp:
        *   D5: [0, out] (DZ33)
    *   *Self-Correction*: The bridge provided in the prompt is `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`. This is a full bridge.

    *   S1: [pzp, n1], C1: [n1, 0], D1: [n1, out], S2: [pzn, n2], C2: [n2, 0], D2: [n2, out].
    *   Wait, the SECE structure is usually: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Switch $\rightarrow$ $C_{ext}$ $\rightarrow$ Diode $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
    *   For both half-cycles:
        *   S1 [pzp, n1], C1 [n1, 0], D1 [n1, out]
        *   S2 [pzn, n2], C2 [n2, 0], D2 [n2, out]
        *   S1 and S2 controlled by G1 and G2 (or one G1 with different edges).
    *   This might be too complex for a first try. Let's stick to SSHI-Bridge and FBR+Zener.

    *   S3 $V_{max}$ is the main problem. DZ33 is a 3.3V zener.
    *   S2 and S4 $V_{avg}$ are the other problems.
    *   SSHI increases $V_{avg}$.
    *   Let's try:
        1.  **FBR + Zener** (Simple, fixes $V_{max}$).
        2.  **SSHI + FBR + Zener** (Advanced, fixes $V_{max}$ and $V_{avg}$).
        3.  **Half-Wave SSHI** (Less components, check if it works).

    *   Let's re-verify the SSHI bridge connectivity.
        *   S1 and L1 in series across the piezo.
        *   D1-D4 as a full bridge.
        *   S1 closes at peaks.
        *   Wait, if the bridge is always there, does the inductor flip work?
        *   In a standard SSHI, the flip happens, and then the energy is harvested.
        *   Actually, the most common "simple" SSHI is:
            Piezo $\rightarrow$ Bridge $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
            Inductor and switch are used to flip $C_p$ *after* the peak.
            The bridge is connected to the piezo.
            The switch $S$ and inductor $L$ are in parallel with the piezo.
            When $S$ closes, $C_p$ resonates with $L$.
            This flips the voltage $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$.
            This flip causes a large current to flow through the bridge diodes, charging $C_{out}$.

    *   Wait, if I use the FBR bridge: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        If pzp is positive, D1 conducts. If pzn is positive, D2 conducts.
        If we flip the voltage (pzp goes from $+$ to $-$), then D3 or D4 will conduct.
        This sounds correct.

    *   S1: [pzp, n1]
    *   L1: [n1, pzn]
    *   G1: SYNC (edges="both", ton=pi*sqrt(L*Cp), phase=0)
    *   D1: [pzp, out] (DSCH)
    *   D2: [pzn, out] (DSCH)
    *   D3: [0, pzp] (DSCH)
    *   D4: [0, pzn] (DSCH)
    *   Cout: [out, 0]
    *   Dz: [0, out] (DZ33)

    *   *Check component count*: 1 S, 1 L, 1 SYNC, 4 D (bridge), 1 D (zener), 1 C = 9 components. (Max 16).

    *   FBR had $V_{max} = 5.72$V (S3) and $V_{avg} = 1.51$V (S4).
    *   The Zener DZ33 will clamp $V_{max}$ to $\sim 3.3$-$3.6$V.
    *   The SSHI flip will increase the $V_{avg}$ for S4 and S2.

    *   Design 1: "FBR_Zener" (FBR + DZ33). Fixes $V_{max}$, maybe not $V_{avg}$.
    *   Design 2: "SSHI_FBR_Zener" (SSHI + FBR + DZ33). Fixes both.
    *   Design 3: "HalfWave_SSHI_Zener" (Half-wave rectifier + SSHI + DZ33).

    *   Let's refine Design 1 (FBR_Zener):
        *   D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]
        *   C1: [out, 0]
        *   D5: [0, out] (DZ33)
    *   Let's refine Design 2 (SSHI_FBR_Zener):
        *   D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]
        *   C1: [out, 0]
        *   D5: [0, out] (DZ33)
        *   S1: [pzp, n1], L1: [n1, pzn], G1: SYNC

    *   Let's refine Design 3 (Parallel-SSHI / SECE-like):
        *   S1: [pzp, n1], C1: [n1, 0], D1: [n1, out]
        *   S2: [pzn, n2], C2: [n2, 0], D2: [n2, out]
        *   G1: SYNC (pos), G2: SYNC (neg)
        *   Cout: [out, 0]
        *   D3: [0, out] (DZ33)
        *   *Wait*, the SECE needs a way to dump the capacitor. Usually, the switch connects the piezo to the capacitor, and the capacitor is connected to the output via a diode.
        *   Actually, a simpler SECE:
            S1 [pzp, n1], C1 [n1, 0], D1 [n1, out].
            When S1 is closed, C1 charges to Vpzp.
            When S1 is open, C1 discharges through D1 into Cout.
            But this only works if Vc1 > Vout.
            This requires the piezo to reach a higher voltage than the output.
            Given $V_{oc} \approx 3.2$V and $V_{out} \approx 1.8$-$3.6$V, this is tight.

    *   Let's stick to the SSHI-FBR-Zener and a simple FBR-Zener. For the third, maybe a "Half-Bridge" version of SSHI to see if it's more efficient? No, let's try a "Charge-Pump" or "Voltage Doubler" style?
    *   Actually, a "Voltage Doubler" (Greinacher circuit) might help S4.
        *   C1: [pzp, n1], D1: [n1, 0], D2: [n1, out], C2: [out, 0].
        *   This is for AC. For piezo, we'd need to use pzn as well.

    *   Let's go with:
        1.  `fbr_zener`: FBR + Zener (Baseline + Clamp)
        2.  `sshi_fbr_zener`: SSHI + FBR + Zener (Voltage boost + Clamp)
        3.  `sshi_half_zener`: Half-wave rectifier + SSHI + Zener (Comparing half vs full bridge)

    *   *Correction on SSHI*: The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ should be in parallel with the piezo.
        S1: [pzp, n1], L1: [n1, pzn], G1: SYNC.
        This means when S1 is closed, we have a loop pzp $\rightarrow$ S1 $\rightarrow$ L1 $\rightarrow$ pzn $\rightarrow$ piezo $\rightarrow$ pzp. This is exactly what is needed to flip the charge on $C_p$.
